slides.label: Area As An Invariant
slides.notes: Open by naming the chapter's governing problem: figures can be congruent, equal in content, equal by a numerical area, or equal by a finite dissection. The lecture follows those notions from planar polygons to circles and finally to volume, where the same story breaks in a precise way.

slides.label: Route Through Chapter 5
slides.notes: Use this route map to keep the chapter from feeling like a list of classical facts. Each stop introduces an invariant and a permitted operation: additive measure, cutting and moving pieces, exhaustion by polygons, and the Dehn ledger for spatial solids.

slides.label: What An Area Function Must Remember
slides.notes: Present area as a bookkeeping rule rather than a formula for special shapes. Positivity prevents invisible nonempty pieces, congruence invariance makes rigid motion irrelevant, and additivity is what allows diagrams to be decomposed without changing the total.

slides.label: Additivity Ledger
slides.notes: Read the figure from left to right as a physical audit of additivity. The same polygon is split into triangles, each triangle carries its own area entry, and the ledger asserts that recombining entries is not an extra theorem but part of the definition of a measure function.

slides.label: Equal Content Versus Equal Area
slides.notes: Separate two ideas that students often blur. Equal content is inherited from Euclidean common notions and dissection-like reasoning, while a measure function assigns a number; Chapter 5 explains when these languages agree and where assumptions such as Archimedes enter.

slides.label: Dissection Is Constructive Equality
slides.notes: Stress that dissection equivalence is more demanding than a matching number because it asks for a finite inventory of pieces and rigid motions. The visual shows the proof habit: cut a figure into named components, move each component, and check that no area is created or lost.

slides.label: Triangle To Parallelogram
slides.notes: Use the triangle-to-parallelogram move as the local engine behind many area formulas. Duplicating or rearranging a triangle makes base and height visible, so the familiar one-half base times height formula becomes a consequence of a rigid piece accounting.

slides.label: Bolyai-Gerwien Roadmap
slides.notes: Frame Bolyai-Gerwien as a theorem about the equivalence of two tests for rectilinear figures in an Archimedean Euclidean plane. The path through triangles, parallelograms, and rectangles matters because it is a constructive route, not a black-box comparison of real numbers.

slides.label: Archimedes At The Boundary
slides.notes: This slide explains why a hidden axiom appears in a chapter about area. Finite dissections cannot always overcome infinitesimal or infinitely displaced geometry, so the Archimedean condition is the bridge from numerical equality to a finite cutting procedure.

slides.label: Circles Need Exhaustion
slides.notes: When the boundary is curved, a finite rectilinear dissection is no longer the natural first language. Inscribed and circumscribed polygons trap the circle, and doubling the number of sides makes the annular error shrink; the area statement is therefore limiting, not a squaring construction.

slides.label: Quadrature Bounds
slides.notes: Use the bound table as a computational version of exhaustion. The inequalities show that the circle's area is squeezed between polygonal areas, and the shrinking gap is what justifies treating the limiting value as the area of the disk.

slides.label: Volume Repeats The Pattern
slides.notes: Move deliberately from planar area to volume without pretending nothing changes. Prisms behave like the polygonal story, while pyramids already require an exhaustion or limiting argument, so three dimensions inherit both the promise and the fragility of the planar theory.

slides.label: Hilbert's Third Problem
slides.notes: State the shock clearly: equal volume is not enough for scissors congruence in three dimensions. A cube and a regular tetrahedron can be scaled to match volume, but a second invariant survives cutting and blocks a dissection between them.

slides.label: Dehn Ledger
slides.notes: Explain the Dehn invariant as an edge-length and angle ledger rather than as a mysterious formula. Cutting subdivides edges and redistributes dihedral angles, but the total class remains unchanged, so a mismatch proves that no finite dissection can exist.

slides.label: One-Cut Shear Lab
slides.notes: Use the lab slide to connect the theorem-level discussion to an experiment students can run mentally. A shear preserves determinant area, but a single clean cut works only under extra geometric conditions; this illustrates why equal area alone does not specify a construction.

slides.label: Takeaways
slides.notes: Close by asking students to identify the invariant before choosing a proof strategy. Chapter 5 is not only about formulas for area; it is about which quantities survive the allowed moves and when those quantities are complete.
